answer: Sybil resistance is bought with per-identity cost, not trust. Each agent must run its work inside an attested compute kernel bound to a distinct hardware root and answer randomised pulse probes at unpredictable intervals; a missed pulse burns part of its bond. New identities board at a wharf, posting stake plus a sponsor's liability that is slashed once clustering exposes shared kernels or synchronised pulse failures. Faking N agents therefore costs N kernels, N stakes and N hits to sponsor reputation, while one honest agent pays once. The attack becomes a linear bill, not cheap bookkeeping.
